newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mortar fire hurts seven at French Bangui embassy.
newsitem.headline: Mortar fire hurts seven at French Bangui embassy.

text.p: Seven people at the French embassy in the Central African Republic were injured on Saturday by two stray mortar shells apparently fired by disaffected soldiers, the French ambassador said.
"No lives are in danger," Jean-Marc Simon told La Chaine Info television by telephone from Bangui. "But one of the staff will have to be repatriated to France...because he has shrapnel in his lungs."
Of the seven injured, five were French nationals and the other two staff from the Central African Republic.

Fresh fighting between African peacekeepers and disaffected soldiers broke out in Bangui on Saturday, killing four civilians and wounding more than 30 including the embassy staff, medical workers and diplomats said.

Simon said the mortars were apparently fired from the Kasai camp, a base for former army mutineers, towards a camp of forces loyal to President Ange-Felix Patasse, a northern civilian elected in 1993.

"As these people are unfortunately very bad shots -- they've shown that already several times -- the shells fell scattered around the upper part of the city of Bangui and two hit the French embassy compound," he said.
He said the attacks showed the urgency of disarming ex-mutineers who have not returned to barracks despite a January 25 peace deal after three uprisings in less than a year.
The first mutinies, in April and May 1996, began as protests over pay but became a movement to topple Patasse. The third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.

French troops, in the country under a defence pact, restored order after the latest mutiny and handed over to the peacekeepers. The African force includes soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo.
